name: aklomp/base64 (SIMD Base64 C99 library)
workload: Single-threaded base64 decode of real files (images, text, 1.4-330 KB) with error checking, from the Muła & Lemire paper; plus encode/decode of a 1 MB buffer from the Turbo-Base64 README shootout
claimed_speedup: Muła & Lemire (ACM TWEB 2018) Table VI, decode on real files: AVX2 (Klomp) 0.43 cycles/byte vs Google Chrome base64 1.8 and Linux kernel base64 20 on lena.jpg (~4.2x vs Chrome, ~46x vs Linux, derived from page data). Also Turbo-Base64 README (1 MB buffer, i7-9700K, gcc 11.2): b64avx2 26,153 MB/s encode / 22,515 MB/s decode vs Google Chrome base64 2,541/4,289 MB/s (~10x encode, ~5x decode, derived from page data)

name: fastbase64 (lemire)
baseline: base64 (glibc/Linux base64 utility and Google Chrome's base64 implementation)
workload: Single-threaded base64 decoding of real base64 payloads: the lena, peppers and mandril JPEGs, a Moby Dick quote, and Google and Bing inline images. Encoding and decoding of random data of varying size. Measured in cycles per input byte with rdtsc, Turbo Boost disabled, minimum of 500 runs. Secondary: 1 MB encode/decode in the Turbo-Base64 README table.
claimed_speedup: Paper (i7-6700, GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native): for large random inputs the AVX2 codec uses about 0.25 cycles per input byte, against Chrome's codec at about 2.7 (encode) and 1.8 (decode). The paper calls this 'eleven times faster at encoding and over seven times faster at decoding'. In Table VI, decoding real files takes 0.21-0.27 cycles/byte against Chrome's 1.8-2.1 (lena: 0.21 vs 1.8). In an independent table in the Turbo-Base64 README (i7-9700K, gcc 11.2, 1 MB), fb64avx2 runs at 23,686/21,231 MB/s encode/decode against Google Chrome base64 at 2,541/4,289 MB/s (about 9.3x encode and 4.9x decode, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 5.3, -O3 -march=native (paper; the repo Makefile also sets -O3 -march=native -mavx2). Turbo-Base64 table: gcc 11.2, no flags stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, Turbo Boost disabled, 32 GB DDR4-2133 (paper); Intel i7-9700K @ 3.6 GHz (Turbo-Base64 table)
tradeoffs: No declared license (NOASSERTION) — can be studied/reimplemented but not copied; project archived, no further maintenance
caveats: The paper's numbers date from 2017. The repo is archived, and its README says it is unmaintained research code, not for production, and that users should switch to simdutf. The AVX2 codec needs AVX2 hardware and falls back to scalar code for short inputs (under about 100 bytes it gains nothing). Turbo-Base64's source comments call fastbase64 'unsafe, can reads/writes beyound i/o buffers'; that is a competitor's claim and is unverified.
found_via: Cross-referenced from Turbo-Base64 README shootout table
GitHub: gh api repos/lemire/fastbase64 (referenced in Turbo-Base64 README 'References')

The paper benchmarks the codec against Chrome's codec (src/chromiumbase64.c) using benchmarks/basic_benchmark.c, and it states GNU GCC 5.3, -O3 -march=native and an Intel i7-6700, so every tier A condition is met. The cited Turbo-Base64 page on its own would support only C, because its comparison harness is not public and it gives no flags.
verification.notes: I moved the evidence to the peer-reviewed paper, whose artifact is this repo. The Turbo-Base64 numbers in the original claim are accurate and belong to the fb64avx2 row, but that harness is closed and gives no flags. name: Faster Base64 Encoding/Decoding using AVX2 (base64simd)
workload: Single-threaded encoding/decoding of byte streams to/from base64 on a Skylake processor, measured in CPU cycles per input byte, vs Google Chrome's base64 codec
claimed_speedup: Paper: for large random inputs the AVX2 codec uses about 0.25 cycles per input byte, against Chrome's codec at about 2.7 (encode) and 1.8 (decode). The paper calls this 'eleven times faster at encoding and over seven times faster at decoding'; the abstract rounds to about 10x and 7x. In Table VI, decoding real files takes 0.21-0.27 cycles/byte against Chrome's 1.8-2.1. The repo README, comparing against its own scalar code only, reports 2-4x faster encoding and 2-2.7x faster decoding.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, Turbo Boost disabled, 32 kB L1d / 256 kB L2 / 8 MB L3 (paper Section 5)
stars_or_usage: 172 stars; underlying algorithm merged into simdutf (Node.js, Chromium, WebKit)
tradeoffs: Requires x86 SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 or ARM NEON; falls back to scalar on unsupported CPUs; strict base64 validation
caveats: The paper's measured codec and its benchmark harness are in lemire/fastbase64; this repo is Muła's research harness of algorithm variants (SSE, AVX2, AVX-512, BMI2, NEON, XOP), each benchmarked only against its own scalar versions. Its README says the code does not process the data tail or '=' padding, so it is not a spec-complete codec; it points users to aklomp/base64 and lemire/fastbase64 for that. The paper, the algorithm and the Chrome comparison are the same as in the lemire/fastbase64 record.

name: aHash
baseline: xxHash (XXH3 via xxhash-rust) and wyhash; also SipHash-1-3, the Rust std HashMap default
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks that hash a u64 and strings of 1-1023 bytes through Rust's Hasher/BuildHasher trait (compare/tests/compare.rs), compared with SipHash, FxHash, FnvHash, FarmHash, HighwayHash, MetroHash, t1ha, xxh3 and wyhash. The "50GB/s" figure comes from the SMHasher bulk test (smhasher/ahashOutput.txt: 60349 MiB/s average at a nominal "3 ghz")
claimed_speedup: Page text (verbatim): "AHash is faster than either one [t1ha and XXHash], both with and without AES"; "AHash outperforms wyHash across all input sizes"; "At over 50GB/s aHash is the fastest algorithm to pass the full test suite by more than a factor of 2"; about 10x faster than SipHash. The Google Sheet linked from the page gives time to hash a u64 and a 1 KB string (units not labelled, probably ns): AHash 0.87 / 19.98, XXHash (xxh3) 11.88 / 114.14, WyHash 1.53 / 53.13, SipHash-1-3 9.70 / 219.13, FxHash 0.71 / 121.97. That makes aHash about 13.7x / 5.7x faster than xxh3, 1.76x / 2.66x faster than wyhash, and 11x / 11x faster than SipHash-1-3 (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: rustc (version unstated); bench profile in compare/Cargo.toml: opt-level=3, lto='fat', codegen-units=1, debug-assertions=false; Criterion 0.3.3; target-cpu/RUSTFLAGS unstated
stars_or_usage: 1347 GitHub stars; about 790M crates.io downloads (about 151M recent) and 2051 reverse dependencies. It was hashbrown's default hasher until hashbrown v0.15.0 (2024-10), which switched to foldhash. It was never the Rust std HashMap default, which is SipHash-1-3.
tradeoffs: Output is not fixed/standardized across hardware and versions, so unsuitable for persisted or transmitted hashes; DOS-resistance relies on per-process random keys.
caveats: No CPU model or rustc version is stated, and the sheet does not label its time units. Comparisons go through Rust Hasher-trait wrappers, which may penalise streaming hashes such as xxh3 on 1 KB inputs. The independent rurban/SMHasher table (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) contradicts the bulk-speed claims: ahash64 9862.62 MiB/s against xxh3 20853.74 and wyhash 22640.53. It shows aHash only slightly ahead on small keys (27.32 cycles/hash against 29.46 for xxh3 and 28.91 for wyhash). The "fastest SMHasher-passing algorithm by >2x" claim is stale. Output is not stable across platforms or versions (HashMap use only). FxHash is faster on u64 keys, as the page admits.

The one independent suite, rurban/SMHasher, does not back the win: it shows aHash losing about 2x on bulk throughput to xxh3 and wyhash and winning only slightly on small keys, so this cannot be B.

Independent SMHasher data contradicts the bulk-throughput superiority claim, so tier stays C with a strong caveat.

name: MuseAir (C++ port)
workload: SMHasher3 small-key (1-31 byte) and bulk (262144-byte) speed tests, run on a 12th Gen Intel i7-12700K, comparing MuseAir/MuseAir-BFast against wyhash and rapidhash
claimed_speedup: Not faster than wyhash overall. On 1-31 byte keys the README chart shows MuseAir and MuseAir-BFast using more cycles per hash than wyhash and rapidhash at almost every length (about 18.6 vs 15.1 cycles at 1-4 bytes, about 35-45 vs 27 at 17-31 bytes). In bulk (262144-byte keys) standard MuseAir is on par with wyhash v4.2 at about 34 GiB/s @ 3.5 GHz. The BFast line appears to be about 42 GiB/s, roughly 1.2x wyhash (read from chart; line colours repeat, so approximate). The README text claims 'up to 33.2 GiB/s' for BFast and that MuseAir 'holds its own against' wyhash, which is a parity claim.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.3.0 (MSYS on Windows), from the SMHasher3 cmake log in the README; flags and build type not stated
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12700K (Windows/MSYS); GiB/s figures assume 3.5 GHz
tradeoffs: requires C++20; header-only but with platform-specific assembly on critical paths; this is a third-party reimplementation, not the canonical original (eternal-io/museair, Rust, no stated license)
caveats: This is a third-party C++20 port of eternal-io/museair (Rust), which is a separate catalog candidate. By the port's own charts it is slower than wyhash and rapidhash on small keys; only BFast bulk hashing looks faster. The README's 33.2 GiB/s text does not match its bulk chart (about 42 GiB/s). SMHasher3's upstream results (MuseAir.bfast 8.64 bytes/cycle bulk and 26.28 cycles for small keys, against wyhash's 6.98 and 29.31) come from SMHasher3's own CC0 MuseAir v0.3 code, not from this port. On licensing, the top badge says 'GNU' and the README License section says MIT, but the LICENSE file is GPL-3.0 (used here).

name: VecFalcon (Vectorized Falcon-Sign)
baseline: C-FN-DSA (Thomas Pornin's FN-DSA/Falcon implementation, github.com/pornin/c-fn-dsa at commit 96e3b92), SHAKE256X4 variant
workload: Falcon-512/1024 sign_core (SHAKE256X4 PRNG variant; SHAKE256X8 on AVX-512F) CPU-cycle medians over 10,000 runs (x86, ARM) or 2,000 runs (RISC-V) across SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512F, NEON, RV64GC, RV64GCB, RV64GCV and RV64GCVB. Also micro-benchmarks of the vectorized BaseSampler and the RVV/RV64D FFT/iFFT.
claimed_speedup: Falcon-512 sign_core cycles vs the C-FN-DSA reference: 1.13x SSE2, 1.23x AVX2, 1.36x AVX-512F, 1.17x NEON, 1.37x RV64GC, 1.36x RV64GCB, 1.58x RV64GCV, 1.59x RV64GCVB (the paper reports these as 13-59% improvements). Falcon-1024: 1.14x-1.59x. The BaseSampler core without PRNG is 4.2x (SSE2), 8.4x (AVX2), 9.8x (AVX-512F), 7.7x (RVV), 3.8x (RV64IM) and 1.8x (NEON) faster than the C-FN-DSA ref core. With PRNG included it is 1.3x-2.7x. RVV FFT/iFFT is 4.1x-4.7x faster than ref on the SpacemiT X60, and RV64D FFT/iFFT is 2.7x-3.0x faster.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (x86-64, Ubuntu 24.04); Clang 10.0.0 (ARM, Ubuntu 20.04); GCC 13.2.0 (RISC-V, Bianbu 1.0.15). All builds use -O2 -DFNDSA_SHAKE256X4=1. x86 builds pin the ISA with -msse2, -mavx2 or -mavx512f plus -mno-* flags for higher extensions. RISC-V builds use -march=rv64gc, rv64gc_zba_zbb, rv64gcv or rv64gcv_zba_zbb.
hardware: Intel i7-11700K (Rocket Lake, 3.6GHz, Turbo Boost and Hyper-Threading disabled); ARM Cortex-A72 (Raspberry Pi 4B, 1.5GHz); SpacemiT X60, RVV v1.0 VLEN=256 (Milk-V Jupiter, 2.0GHz)
license: MIT (root LICENSE). The C-FN-DSA-derived opt/ and ref/ directories carry the Unlicense. opt/fft_neon.c is Apache-2.0 (derived from GMUCERG Falcon_NEON).
stars_or_usage: 4 stars; IACR TCHES 2026 accepted paper artifact
tradeoffs: Baseline is the C-FN-DSA reference implementation, not liboqs's own bundled Falcon backend directly, though the two are architecturally related (liboqs's Falcon derives from the same lineage of reference/optimized code); the vectorized BaseSampler deliberately breaks bit-for-bit KAT reproducibility with official test vectors while preserving verification interoperability
caveats: Gains are for signature generation (sign_core) only, not keygen or verify, and are measured on the SHAKE256X4 variant, which is not KAT-compatible with default Falcon signing (interoperable for verification). Part of the gain comes from integrated third-party code: XKCP 8-way Keccak on AVX-512F; the BK22 hybrid Keccak and NG23 NEON FFT on ARM; ZYHK25 Keccak on RISC-V. The paper measured C-FN-DSA as faster than the NIST-submission AVX2 code on the i7-11700K, so it is a strong baseline. The only direct comparison with other optimized prior work is at the BaseSampler level (NG23 NEON is slower than ref). Licensing is mixed: MIT, Unlicense (public-domain dedication, no patent grant) and Apache-2.0 files. GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION.
found_via: GitHub graphql search: 'falcon signature avx2 in:name,description,readme'

verification.tier_reason: The ePrint 2025/1867 paper (published in TCHES 2026, DOI 10.46586/tches.v2026.i1.302-324) benchmarks sign_core against the C-FN-DSA reference at commit 96e3b92 (Table 6) and states the compiler (GCC 13.3.0, Clang 10.0.0, GCC 13.2.0), the flags (-O2, -DFNDSA_SHAKE256X4=1, per-ISA -m/-march flags) and the CPUs (i7-11700K, Cortex-A72, SpacemiT X60). The artifact repo ships the benchmark code for both sides (opt/speed_fndsa.c and ref/speed_fndsa.c with per-platform Makefiles, plus profiling/ for BaseSampler and FFT) and the raw outputs (opt/ and ref/speed_fndsa_*.txt), which match Table 6.
verification.notes: All claimed numbers check out against Tables 4-6 of the paper and the repo's raw speed files. The one overstatement was 'up to 8.4x faster than prior work': 8.4x is the AVX2 BaseSampler core vs the C-FN-DSA ref, and the maximum is 9.8x on AVX-512F. The record's metric is 'throughput', but the paper measures per-signature cycle latency. Metadata verified: 4 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2025-12-05 (active), usability copyable (all components are under OSI licenses).
